patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 5/5] x86/paravirt: Trace contended_release on unlock
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the unlock path for PARAVIRT_SPINLOCKS=y kernels by swapping the target of a static_call() to a traced unlock when the contended_release tracepoint is enabled. This reduces overhead when tracing is disabled, as it avoids a branch that would otherwise be taken even if tracing is off. The patch also introduces two new traced unlock variants and updates the pv_is_native_spin_unlock function accordingly.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 4/5] tracing/lock: Use TRACE_EVENT_FN() for contended_release
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the tracing of lock contention events in Linux by using a new macro, TRACE_EVENT_FN(), for the contended_release event. This change allows for more flexibility and customization when tracing this specific event. The patch introduces weak no-op hooks for architectures to override if they need custom behavior. Currently, these hooks are empty, resulting in no functional changes until an architecture overrides them.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 3/5] locking/qspinlock: Add contended_release tracepoint
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch adds a contended_release tracepoint to the qspinlock locking mechanism, allowing for attribution of contended spinlocks to their holders. The patch combines contention check, trace call, and release into an out-of-line function to minimize overhead. It also introduces a new configuration option to enable or disable this feature. The patch aims to provide more detailed information about lock contention in the Linux kernel.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 2/5] locking: Factor out queued_spin_release()
patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch introduces a new function, queued_spin_release(), which is an arch-overridable release primitive for spinlocks. It creates a generic wrapper around the existing queued_spin_unlock() function, allowing architectures to customize only the release behavior if needed. The MIPS architecture's override is renamed to match this change, but x86 paravirt remains unchanged as it directly overrides queued_spin_unlock(). This patch does not introduce any functional changes and is intended to facilitate future tracing and debugging efforts.

patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH 1/5] x86/paravirt: Use static_call() for the paravirt spinlock ops

version_history.subject: [PATCH 1/5] x86/paravirt: Use static_call() for the paravirt spinlock ops

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch replaces the use of paravirt-ops ALTERNATIVE machinery for dispatching spinlock operations on x86 architecture with static_call(). This change allows the target function to be updated at runtime, which is necessary for implementing a contended_release tracepoint. The patch updates several files in the kernel and includes changes to support module safety and boot testing on native and KVM PV guest systems.

review_comments.author: Matthew Wilcox
review_comments.summary: Provided a detailed explanation of why it's safe to proceed without holding a reference on the page, citing existing code and logic.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Tue, Aug 04, 2026 at 03:15:37PM -0400, Gregory Price wrote:
> On Fri, Jul 31, 2026 at 09:07:55PM +0100, Matthew Wilcox (Oracle) wrote:
> > +/*
> > + * We have no reference on the folio containing this page.
> > + * The hugetlb_lock keeps hugetlb folios from being freed.
> > + */
> > +bool hugetlb_unref_page_hwpoison(const struct page *page)
> > +{
> > +	const struct folio *folio;
> > +	unsigned long flags;
> > +	bool ret;
> > +
> > +	spin_lock_irqsave(&hugetlb_lock, flags);
> > +	folio = page_folio(page);
> > +	if (!folio_test_huge_poison(folio)) {
> > +		ret = PageHWPoison(page);
> > +		goto unlock;
> > +	}
> > +
> > +	ret = precise_page_poisoned(folio, page);
> > +unlock:
> > +	spin_unlock_irqrestore(&hugetlb_lock, flags);
> > +	return ret;
> > +}
> > +
> 
> I ended up with the same question as sashiko - i think this behavior
> implies we must hold a reference on the page, otherwise the folio can
> be invalid and all these accesses are unsafe.
> 
> But that must be the existing behavior for poison checks like this, so
> this is at least no worse. Not sure it's worth addressing.

Let me just paste Sashiko's comment in here so we preserve it in the
lore archives and so we're definitely talking about the same thing:

> This is a pre-existing issue, but does calling page_folio()
> here without holding a reference to the page risk a panic during
> lockless PFN scanning?  If a monitoring tool reads /proc/kpageflags or
> /proc/kcore, pfn_to_online_page() retrieves the page without acquiring
> a reference. If the page is concurrently freed and reallocated for
> driver use, compound_info (which aliases lru.next) could be modified.
> Could this cause page_folio() to misidentify the page as a tail page
> and return an invalid folio pointer, leading to an out-of-bounds memory
> read when folio_test_huge_poison() accesses folio->page.page_type?
> While the hugetlb_lock is held here, can it stabilize unreferenced
> pages that might have already been repurposed into non-hugetlb pages?

Sashiko is mistaken (... and fair enough, I suspect you aren't the only
human who's confused by this either)

It's quite right that we can observe a page in literally any state since
we do not hold a refcount.  But it is forbidden to use bit 0 of lru.next
for any purpose other than indicating "this is a tail page":

       /*
         * Five words (20/40 bytes) are available in this union.
         * WARNING: bit 0 of the first word is used for PageTail(). That
         * means the other users of this union MUST NOT use the bit to
         * avoid collision and false-positive PageTail().
         */

That's been the rule since 2015 with commit 1d798ca3f164

So the pointer we get back from page_folio() must have been a folio _at
some point_.  It may not be a folio now.  It may be a folio, but not one
that contains this page.  But it's not a wild pointer, and treating it
as if it's a folio won't cause any harm (as long as we're really careful).

Specifically, we call:

> +	if (!folio_test_huge_poison(folio)) {

and all that does is access folio->page.page_type aka mapcount.  So if
the pointer we have is not a current folio, it'll just return false and
we'll check PageHWPoison.

So the only case this can return 'true' is if the folio was hugetlb
at that exact point.  And we've got the hugetlb lock, so it can't stop
being a hugetlb folio.  At this point it's safe to walk the list.

That's my reasoning, and I think Sashiko has explained enough of its
reasoning to be fairly sure Sashiko is wrong about this.  But hey,
you're not Sashiko.  Maybe you've found a gap in my logic.

series_items.patch_summary: The patch series aims to optimize memory allocation in the btrfs_insert_orphan_item() function by allocating a small struct on the stack instead of dynamically, reducing the risk of transaction aborts due to memory failures.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/5] btrfs: split btrfs_insert_delayed_dir_index() into prealloc and commit phases
series_items.patch_summary: This patch splits the btrfs_insert_delayed_dir_index() function into three separate functions: prealloc, commit, and free. The prealloc function allocates memory for a delayed node and item before modifying the B-tree, allowing -ENOMEM to be returned cleanly if allocation fails. The commit function populates the item data and inserts it into the rb-tree, while the free function releases pre-allocated resources in case of failure. This refactoring improves error handling and reduces the risk of aborting transactions due to memory allocation failures.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/5] btrfs: pre-allocate delayed dir index before btree modification
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the Btrfs file system by pre-allocating delayed directory indices before modifying the btree. This change prevents ENOMEM failures from leaving the btree in an inconsistent state, which could only be resolved by aborting the transaction. The patch introduces a new parameter to the btrfs_insert_dir_item function for caller-provided pre-allocation and removes a wrapper function that was no longer needed.

review_comments.author: Qu Wenruo
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Qu Wenruo noted that when a pre-allocated delayed dir index is passed to btrfs_insert_dir_item(), and an ENOMEM failure occurs before insert_with_overflow() is called, the pre-alloc memory is leaked because it is not properly released.

Reviewer Qu Wenruo noted that the preallocated memory in btrfs_prealloc_delayed_dir_index() is not utilizing the name->name field, and suggested merging the subsequent memcpy() into this function to avoid unnecessary copying.
review_comments.raw_body:
This is exposed by sashiko.

If we have @prealloc passed in, and before we even hit 
insert_with_overflow(), the previous btrfs_alloc_path() failed, we 
return -ENOMEM directly, leaking the @prealloc.

---

Sashiko also pointed out that, the preallocation itself doesn't really 
utilize name->name.

Thus it may be a good idea to merge the later memcpy() into the 
preallocation function.

Thanks,
Qu

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/5] btrfs: handle ENOMEM from btrfs_insert_dir_item() without aborting
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Btrfs kernel code to handle ENOMEM errors from btrfs_insert_dir_item() without aborting the transaction. Instead of aborting, it clears the nlink count and orphans the newly-created inode when memory is exhausted during file system operations such as create(), mkdir(), mknod(), symlink(), and link(). This change allows for more graceful handling of memory pressure situations, preventing potential filesystem corruption.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 5/5] btrfs: pre-allocate delayed dir index for non-overwrite rename
series_items.patch_summary: This patch improves the Btrfs file system by pre-allocating a delayed directory index before performing non-overwrite renames, allowing for early detection of ENOMEM errors and preventing potential data corruption. The patch introduces a new function to pre-allocate the delayed dir index and modifies existing functions to handle this new parameter. It also preserves the current behavior for overwrite renames by continuing with the transaction even if an ENOMEM error is encountered.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses a long-standing issue in the Btrfs file system where memory allocation failures can cause the file system to abort. The patches rework the code to perform memory allocations before critical points, preventing aborts due to ENOMEM errors. This includes changes to directory morphing and orphan handling, with additional tests added to exercise the new behavior. While not all potential cases are covered, this series is designed to work in conjunction with other patches to address remaining issues.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/2] nfsd: fix type mismatch and explain host-endian xdr buffer usage
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a type mismatch in the nfsd code and clarifies how host-endian xdr buffers are used. The issue was identified by sparse, which flagged a type mismatch. The patch also explains why the xdr buffer usage is non-standard.

review_comments.author: Chuck Lever
review_comments.summary: Reviewer Chuck Lever expressed confusion about the patch's xdr buffer usage, specifically questioning why host-order bytes are being stored in an XDR stream and suggesting that the code should be rewritten to follow standard practices.
review_comments.raw_body:
I still don't understand what's going on. "Steal a few words to hold it"
sounds like you're trying to avoid a kmalloc call. Is this code reserving
space in the XDR stream, or isn't it? If it is, then accessing those bytes
has to be done with a big-endian pointer, the same way it is done at every
other xdr_reserve_space() call site. Storing host-order bytes that are not
part of an opaque into an XDR stream is just... wrong.

If you're doing the usual "reserve and backfill the encoded data later"
dance, then spell it the way everyone else does so us poor human readers
can recognize that's what's going on.


-- 
Chuck Lever

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary: The author is addressing Chuck Lever's concern about the use of host-endian xdr buffer, specifically reserving a small piece of the buffer to hold bitmap fields that will be encoded later. The author disagrees with the issue and asks for elaboration on why this is problematic.
review_comments.raw_body:
It's using a small piece of the xdr buffer (3 32-bit words) to hold the
host-endian bitmap fields that will later be encoded into the stream
when the encoding is actually done.

This piece is not accessed by anything else and there is plenty of room
in the buffer, so I don't see the issue here. Can you elaborate on why
you feel that this is a problem?
 
Certainly we could do this with yet another set of separate
allocations, but I'm not clear on how we'd track them to free them.
Each notify_entry4 gets a separate bitmap, so we'd need more than one.

-- 
Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>

review_comments.author: Chuck Lever
review_comments.summary:
The reviewer, Chuck Lever, expressed concerns about the patch being a 'hack' and technical debt due to unclear code, and warned that using the XDR stream buffer as temporary storage is not wise and may cause issues in future changes.

Reviewer suggested using temporary allocations on the server-side to match the client-side behavior, allowing for earlier cleanup of resources.
review_comments.raw_body:
Well A-number-1 is that it's a hack and technical debt. It just
isn't obvious what's going on, it needs a four-line comment to
explain it, and it opens the door to people copy-pasting it to
other encoders.

Number 2 is that the XDR stream buffer is ephemeral. There are
conditions that callers must stick to to keep that pointer valid
for the lifetime of the xdr_stream.

Number 3: Yes, we have a sordid history of grabbing a piece of
the xdr_buf's tail iov for temporary storage. That doesn't make
it wise to do, and assumes behavior about that buffer that is
not guaranteed by sunrpc's API contracts. That makes life hard
when future changes need to change that buffer to, say, a page
rather than kmalloc'd memory. Or when I want to convert this
code to use xdrgen instead of hand-rolled encoding.

So what you've done is fine for operational prototype code, but
not something we can carry forward as production code. The sparse
warning is a canary, it's not the actual structural problem.

---

The server has a chain of temporary allocations that are freed
after the COMPOUND is released. Could do something similar for
the server's callback client.


-- 
Chuck Lever

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary:
Author addressed a concern about memory allocation for attrmask, explaining that these allocations only need to stick around until encoding is done and have the same lifetime as the xdr buffer itself.

Author disputes reviewer's claim that host-endian xdr buffer usage is non-standard, stating it has not been communicated as forbidden in previous reviews.

Author responded to Chuck Lever's question about whether he intends to drop the dir delegation series again, explaining that reworking host-endian field allocation is a substantial effort.
review_comments.raw_body:
We only need these allocations to stick around until the encoding is
done. They have almost the same lifetime as the xdr buffer itself which
is why allocating from it made sense.

---

I had no idea this practice was suddenly forbidden. That has certainly
not been communicated to me in any of the previous review rounds over
the last couple of years.

---

Does this mean you intend to drop dir delegation series again?

Allocating from the xdr stream in order to hold host-endian fields is
done in several places in this code. Reworking that will be a
substantial effort.
-- 
Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>

review_comments.author: Chuck Lever
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer Chuck Lever noted that the patch introduces a host-endian xdr buffer usage pattern, which he has previously removed from other codebases, and requested an explanation of why this is done.

reviewer noted that the patch's fix for type mismatch in nfsd4xdr.c is not an urgent issue, as it is not causing immediate problems or vulnerabilities
sentiment_signals: not an immediate on-the-wire behavioral problem
review_comments.raw_body:
I've been removing instances of this anti-pattern for some time. I
haven't seen new code (until now) that tries to do this. It simply
hasn't come up recently and I typically don't look closely for it.

---

No. It's deep in nfsd-next now, and this is a long-term issue, not
an immediate on-the-wire behavioral problem or a vulnerability.


-- 
Chuck Lever

review_comments.author: Jeff Layton (author)
review_comments.summary: Author acknowledged that the type mismatch fix needs more work and testing, promising a follow-up patch in a separate series.
review_comments.raw_body:
Ok. I had an LLM draft up a propsed fix for this, but it's a bit
invasive and needs more testing. I'll see if I can put something
together in a follow-on series to the CB_NOTIFY patches.
-- 
Jeff Layton <jlayton@kernel.org>
